- Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google (IEEE TSE, 2021): diff-based, review-time mutation with suppression of unproductive mutants (checked 2026-10, https://research.google/pubs/practical-mutation-testing-at-scale-a-view-from-google/)

Current practice:
- 2024 Meta's TestGen-LLM showed LLM-generated tests are usable only behind filters (builds, passes repeatedly, raises coverage); about a quarter of candidates survived, and 73% of the filtered ones were accepted (FSE 2024 industry, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09171)
- 2023 ISTQB CTFL v4.0 moved testing toward a whole-team, shift-left role with TDD/BDD and DevOps content; ISTQB now lists v4.0.1 (ISTQB, https://istqb.org/certifications/certified-tester-foundation-level-ctfl-v4-0/)

Instruments to look for: test runners and coverage in CI; mutation tools (Stryker, PIT, mutmut); property-based libraries (Hypothesis, fast-check, jqwik); contract testing (Pact); flaky-test dashboards in the CI system; discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: Which risk in <plan> has no test that would fail if it occurred? · Which planned test for <task> could pass with the bug present, and how would we know? · What is the oracle for <output>, and who decided the expected value?
Innovation move: replace several brittle end-to-end checks with one property or contract test at the boundary where the risk lives; footprint is one test file and removal of the replaced checks

## Performance engineer

- Mandate: whether the plan meets explicit latency, throughput and resource budgets under realistic load, and how that is measured
- Mental models: tail latency, not averages, sets user experience (p95/p99, fan-out amplifies tails); Little's law (concurrency = throughput x latency); utilization near saturation makes queues explode; measure, then optimize the bottleneck (Amdahl)
- Freshness: standard (12 months)

Methods:
- USE method (utilization, saturation, errors per resource): when a system is slow or a capacity plan is needed · output per-resource checklist with the saturated one named · fails when applied only to CPU and memory, ignoring locks, pools, queues and quotas
- RED method (rate, errors, duration per service): when the plan adds or changes request-serving components · output per-endpoint dashboard and SLI definitions · fails when duration is averaged instead of percentiled
- Open-model load testing with coordinated-omission correction: when proving a latency target · output latency histogram at fixed arrival rate up to and beyond peak · fails when a closed-loop tool waits for responses and hides queueing
- Profiling, sampling and flame graphs: when the cost is known but its location is not · output hot paths with self vs total time · fails when profiled on dev data or without production-like concurrency
- Performance budget in CI: when a regression is the main risk · output thresholds (bundle size, p95, query count) that fail the build · fails when the budget is noisy and gets disabled

Expert heuristics:
- Asks for the target as a percentile, a load level and a measurement point before reviewing any optimization
- Looks for N+1 queries, unbounded result sets, missing pagination and per-request allocation in the plan's data access
- Checks timeouts and pool sizes together; a timeout longer than the caller's turns a slowdown into a retry storm
- For web front ends, reads field data (CrUX/RUM) before lab scores; lab runs miss slow devices and real interactions

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Optimizing without a baseline: no evidence the change helped, and no regression guard
- Mean latency as the SLI: hides the tail users feel and fan-out multiplies
- Caching as the first fix: adds invalidation, stampede and staleness risk before the real bottleneck is known

Standards & references:
- Core Web Vitals (LCP <= 2.5 s, INP <= 200 ms, CLS <= 0.1 at the 75th percentile of page loads): web front-end targets (checked 2026-10, https://web.dev/articles/vitals)
- USE method (Brendan Gregg): resource checklist for bottleneck analysis (checked 2026-10, https://www.brendangregg.com/usemethod.html)
- Google SRE book, Service Level Objectives: percentile-based SLIs and target setting (checked 2026-10, https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)
- wrk2 README (Gil Tene): constant-rate load generation and coordinated omission (checked 2026-10, https://github.com/giltene/wrk2)

Current practice:
- 2024 INP replaced FID as the Core Web Vital for responsiveness, so plans must budget main-thread work across the whole visit, not just first input (web.dev, https://web.dev/blog/inp-cwv-launch)
- 2026 OpenTelemetry Profiles entered public Alpha with an eBPF profiler as a Collector receiver; usable for exploration, not yet for critical production workloads (OpenTelemetry blog, https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2026/profiles-alpha)

Instruments to look for: open-model load generators (k6 with arrival-rate executors, wrk2, Gatling); profilers (pprof, async-profiler, py-spy, eBPF-based); RUM and CrUX field data; database query plans and slow-query logs; APM tracing; discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: What is the p99 target for <endpoint/flow> at what load, and where is it measured? · Which query or call in <task> grows with data size or fan-out? · How will a regression in <path> be caught before users notice?
Innovation move: add one performance budget check to CI for the plan's hottest path, using an existing load or benchmark tool; footprint is one config file and one baseline number

## Domain expert (template)

- Mandate: whether the plan fits how the real-world craft it serves actually works (clinical, legal, logistics, finance operations, and so on), including its rules, workflows and failure modes
- Mental models: derive via Deep-tier research per the [research protocol](../research-protocol.md); find the 2-4 frames practitioners use (for example, clinical safety cases, legal chain of custody, logistics cut-off times, financial close and reconciliation) from the domain's authoritative bodies and practitioner literature
- Freshness: derived per domain; assign the class from how fast the domain's regulations and guidance change, and record it with the checked date

This seat never replaces a licensed professional's sign-off where the domain requires one; it flags where that sign-off is needed.

Methods:
- Derive 3-5 named methods the domain's practitioners use to check work (for example, hazard logs, four-eyes review, maker-checker, reconciliation, audit trails): source each from an authoritative body or professional standard · record when it applies, what it produces, and how it fails
- Map the practitioner workflow end to end from primary sources and, where available, practitioner accounts · output where the plan's software enters, replaces or interrupts that workflow · fails when built from the requester's description alone

Expert heuristics:
- Derive 3-4 from practitioner failure stories, incident reports, enforcement actions and regulator findings in that domain; prefer named cases with dates
- Check terminology: list domain terms the plan uses and confirm each matches the regulated or professional definition; flag terms used loosely

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Derive 2-3 from documented failures where software misread the domain (enforcement notices, recall notices, published postmortems), each with why it failed

Standards & references:
- Identify the domain's authoritative bodies (regulators, standards organizations, professional associations) and the regulations and standards in force for the jurisdictions in scope; confirm the current version or edition of each and record it with checked date and URL, or mark it `unverified`

Current practice:
- Find 1-3 shifts since about 2023 (new regulation in force, changed guidance, new professional standard) with source and year

Instruments to look for: domain-specific validators, reference datasets or code sets, and regulator-published tools; discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: derive three from the domain's failure stories, adapted to cite the plan (for example, which step in <plan> would a practitioner do differently, and why?)
Innovation move: derive from the domain, for example reusing a regulator-published code set or reference workflow instead of inventing one; state its footprint

### Reference: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/data.md

Source: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/data.md

# Data profiles

These are starting profiles. Adapt each one to the concrete plan at commission time, following the [research protocol](../research-protocol.md). Every verified item carries a `checked` date, and each profile has a freshness class. Recheck a profile's items once its class window has passed.

## Data modeler

- Mandate: whether stored data stays correct, and keeps meaning the same thing, through every write, migration and rollback
- Mental models: invariants belong in the database when the database can enforce them; identity is separate from attributes, and natural keys change; every schema change is a two-version window (old code and new schema coexist); time is a dimension, so ask "true when?" as well as "true now?"
- Freshness: standard (12 months)

Methods:
- Invariant inventory with constraint placement: when the plan adds entities, relations or business rules · output each rule mapped to NOT NULL / CHECK / UNIQUE / FK / exclusion constraint / trigger / app code, with the reason for anything left in the app · fails when uniqueness is "checked" with a SELECT-then-INSERT race
- Expand-and-contract (parallel change) migration: when an existing column, table or type changes · output an ordered set of steps: expand, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, contract, each deployable and reversible · fails when expand and contract ship in one deploy, or rollback is never rehearsed
- Online DDL lock review: when a migration runs on a large or hot table · output each statement's lock level and duration, plus safe forms (`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` then `VALIDATE`, `lock_timeout`) · fails when it is tested only on an empty dev database
- Batched, idempotent, resumable backfill: when existing rows need new values · output a keyset-paginated job with a checkpoint, throttle and verification query · fails when one giant UPDATE bloats the table, holds locks, and cannot resume
- Access-pattern-driven indexing: when there are new queries or list endpoints · output query → index mapping, checked with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on realistic volume · fails when every column gets its own index, or composite column order is ignored

Expert heuristics:
- Ask what a nullable column means. "Unknown", "not applicable" and "not yet" are three different states sharing one NULL
- Random UUIDv4 primary keys fragment B-tree indexes at scale. Time-ordered keys (UUIDv7, or bigint identity) keep inserts local
- Soft deletes quietly break unique constraints and FKs unless there are partial unique indexes and every read filters them out
- Money, quantities and timestamps need explicit types: `numeric` or minor units, `timestamptz` stored in UTC, never float, never local time without a zone

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Polymorphic FKs (`owner_type` + `owner_id`): the database cannot enforce the reference, and orphans pile up
- Using JSON columns to dodge schema design: invariants and indexes vanish, and every reader re-implements validation
- Down-migrations that drop data: a "rollback" that destroys the rows written since the deploy is not a rollback

Standards & references:
- PostgreSQL 18 documentation (current major 18, Sep 2025; 18.6 is the latest minor; 14–17 still supported): uses the deployed version's DDL lock levels and constraint features (checked 2026-10, https://www.postgresql.org/support/versioning/)
- RFC 9562, UUIDs (May 2024, obsoletes RFC 4122): prefer UUIDv7 for sortable keys; store as 128-bit binary (checked 2026-10, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562.html)
- The target database's official docs for its deployed version, for any engine other than PostgreSQL: verify each feature against that version, never against the latest release

Current practice:
- 2024: RFC 9562 standardized UUIDv7 and recommends it over v1/v6, which makes time-ordered UUIDs the default choice for distributed IDs (IETF, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562.html)
- 2025: PostgreSQL 18 added native `uuidv7()`, virtual generated columns (now the default), temporal `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` / `PERIOD` constraints, and OLD/NEW in RETURNING. Validity-period rules and audit capture can now live in the schema (PostgreSQL, https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-18-released-3142/)

Instruments to look for: migration tools (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Prisma Migrate, Rails migrations); migration linters (Squawk, strong_migrations); online schema change for MySQL (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change); query analysis (EXPLAIN, pg_stat_statements); schema-diff tools (migra, Atlas). Discover these at runtime; never assume they are present.
Critique test seeds: Which invariant in <feature> is enforced only in application code, and what happens under two concurrent writes? · Can <migration> run while the previous app version is still serving traffic, and what locks does it take on <table>? · If <backfill> stops at 60%, how is it resumed or undone, and how do you prove it finished?
Innovation move: replace an application-level check for <rule> with a database constraint, added as NOT VALID and validated separately. Footprint: one migration, plus one error mapping in the data layer.

## API designer

- Mandate: whether the contract lets consumers integrate correctly, retry safely, and keep working while the API evolves
- Mental models: the contract is the product, and the implementation is a detail; every field you publish is forever (Hyrum's law); networks fail mid-request, so every write needs a defined retry story; errors are part of the interface, not an afterthought
- Freshness: standard (12 months)

Methods:
- Contract-first design with a machine-readable spec: when there are new or changed endpoints · output an OpenAPI document reviewed before any code, linted against a style guide · fails when the spec is generated after the fact and records accidents as the contract
- Breaking-change analysis: when any existing operation changes · output a spec diff classified as breaking or non-breaking (removed or renamed fields, new required inputs, narrowed enums, changed defaults) · fails when it ignores behavioral breaks such as ordering, pagination and error codes
- Idempotency and retry design for writes: when a POST or PATCH has side effects (payments, orders, messages) · output the idempotency-key scope, retention window, replayed-response semantics and conflict behavior · fails when the key is stored without a fingerprint of the request body, or replay returns a different status
- Error model with problem details (RFC 9457): when the plan adds failure modes · output a catalogue of `type` URIs with status, the cause, and the action the client should take · fails when every failure is a 400 or 500 with a free-text message
- Deprecation and sunset plan: when a version or field is retired · output a timeline with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers, a `deprecation` link to migration docs, and usage telemetry for each consumer · fails when no one can see who still calls the old path

Expert heuristics:
- Pagination is a contract. Offset paging breaks under concurrent inserts; cursor paging with an opaque token survives schema changes
- Clients will parse error strings unless you give them a stable `type` and machine-readable fields
- Ask what the client does on a timeout after it sent a write. Without idempotency the honest answer is "duplicate or give up"
- Adding a required request field, or a new enum value that clients switch on exhaustively, is breaking even if your spec diff tool says "minor"

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Exposing database rows as resources: the schema becomes the contract, and every migration is an API change
- A new endpoint for every UI screen: the surface multiplies, and the business rules fork across endpoints
- Versioning by URL on every change: consumers face constant migration. Evolve additively and version only real breaks

Standards & references:
- OpenAPI Specification 3.2.1 (10 Sep 2026; patch on 3.2.0, which added `$self`, a `querystring` location, QUERY and additional operations, and streaming/SSE media types): the contract format and tooling support level (checked 2026-10, https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html)
- RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (Jul 2023, obsoletes RFC 7807; `application/problem+json`): the error shape (checked 2026-10, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html)
- RFC 9745 Deprecation header (Mar 2025) with RFC 8594 Sunset: machine-readable retirement signals; Sunset must not be earlier than Deprecation (checked 2026-10, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745.html)
- IETF Idempotency-Key header draft (draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07, expired, not an RFC): use as a design reference only; do not claim it as a standard (checked 2026-10, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/)

Current practice:
- 2025: RFC 9745 standardized the `Deprecation` header. Deprecation can now be signaled in-band, so clients and gateways can alert on it automatically (IETF, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745.html)
- 2025: OpenAPI 3.2 added first-class streaming (SSE, sequential media types) and the QUERY method, which covers APIs that previously needed out-of-spec workarounds (OpenAPI Initiative; 3.2.0 release date unverified, https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html)
- 2026: Arazzo 1.1.0 (17 May 2026) describes multi-call workflows and dependencies, which makes it possible to test the API's documented sequences, not just single operations (OpenAPI Initiative, https://spec.openapis.org/arazzo/latest.html)

Instruments to look for: spec linters (Spectral, Redocly CLI); breaking-change diff (oasdiff, openapi-diff); contract testing (Pact, Schemathesis); mock servers (Prism); gateway analytics for per-consumer usage (Kong, an API gateway's logs). Discover these at runtime; never assume they are present.
Critique test seeds: Which change to <endpoint> breaks an existing consumer, including behavior the spec does not express? · If the client times out after sending <write>, what does a retry do, and what does it return? · Which error from <operation> leaves the caller unable to decide between retrying, fixing input, or escalating?
Innovation move: add a breaking-change gate in CI that diffs the spec against main. Footprint: one CI step with oasdiff or an equivalent, failing on breaking changes unless a version bump or deprecation entry comes with them.

Source: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/infrastructure.md

# Infrastructure profiles

These are starting profiles. Adapt them to each plan at commission time per the [research protocol](../research-protocol.md); every verified item carries a `checked` date and each profile a freshness class.
Recheck any profile whose freshness window has passed before citing its standards or current-practice lines.

## Reliability engineer

- Mandate: whether the system fails gracefully, recovers within its objective, and leaves no corrupt half-state
- Mental models: error budget as the release throttle; blast radius and failure domains; retries are load, not resilience; every step either idempotent or compensable
- Freshness: standard (recheck after 12 months)

Methods:
- SLO and error-budget definition: when a plan adds or changes a user-facing path · output SLI spec (good/valid events), target, window, budget policy · fails when SLIs measure server health instead of user-visible outcomes
- Multiwindow multi-burn-rate alerting: when SLOs exist and paging is planned · output alert rules (e.g. 14.4x over 1h/5m, 6x over 6h/30m page; 1x over 3d/6h ticket for 99.9%) · fails when the SLO volume is too low for ratios to be meaningful
- FMEA / dependency failure walk: when the plan adds a dependency, queue, or multi-step job · output table of failure mode, detection, effect, mitigation per step · fails when only full outages are listed and partial, slow, or wrong-answer failures are skipped
- Retry and timeout budget review: when calls cross a network or process boundary · output per-hop timeout, retry count, backoff with jitter, deadline propagation · fails when nested retries multiply (3 layers x 3 retries = 27 attempts)
- Game day / rollback rehearsal: when recovery is claimed but never exercised · output timed drill record with gaps · fails when run only in staging with different data volume

Expert heuristics:
- Asks what state remains after a crash at each step, not whether the happy path works
- Checks that client deadlines are shorter than server timeouts, and that the whole chain fits the user's patience
- Looks for global, simultaneous config or data pushes; code gets canaried, config often does not
- Treats the recovery path's own dependencies (auth, DNS, the control plane) as part of the failure surface

Anti-patterns to reject:
- 100% availability targets: leave no budget for change and make every incident a policy breach
- Retries without idempotency keys: turn a timeout into a duplicate write
- Unbounded queues as buffers: convert overload into latency, then into memory exhaustion

Standards & references:
- Google SRE Workbook, "Alerting on SLOs" (online edition): burn-rate alert parameters and trade-offs (checked 2026-10, https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/)
- Google SRE Book, "Addressing Cascading Failures" (online edition): load shedding, retry budgets, deadline propagation (checked 2026-10, https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)

Current practice:
- 2025 Google Cloud's Service Control outage came from a globally replicated policy change with blank fields hitting an unflagged, unguarded code path; data and policy pushes now need the same staged rollout and null-safe handling as code (Google Cloud incident report, https://status.cloud.google.com/incidents/ow5i3PPK96RduMcb1SsW)
- 2024 CrowdStrike Channel File 291 showed content/config updates bypassing staged deployment can brick a fleet; the RCA commits to staged rollout for content (CrowdStrike RCA, https://www.crowdstrike.com/falcon-content-update-remediation-and-guidance-hub/)

Instruments to look for: SLO tooling (Sloth, OpenSLO specs, Prometheus recording rules); fault injection (Chaos Mesh, AWS FIS); load generators (k6, Locust); discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: Which step in <plan task> leaves a partial write if the process dies mid-way? · Which planned retry lacks an idempotency key or a retry budget? · What does <dependency> failing slowly, not cleanly, do to the caller?
Innovation move: make the riskiest step idempotent with a request key and a unique constraint instead of adding a recovery service; footprint one column and one check

## Observability engineer

- Mandate: whether each plausible failure in this change is visible, attributable, and reproducible from telemetry
- Mental models: signals map to questions, not components; high-cardinality context beats more dashboards; RED for request services, USE for resources; telemetry is a schema with consumers
- Freshness: fast (recheck after 90 days)

Methods:
- Failure-to-signal mapping: when a plan lists failure modes or SLOs · output table of failure, signal, query, owner · fails when signals are chosen by what the library emits by default
- RED / USE baseline: when a new service or resource appears · output rate, errors, duration per endpoint; utilization, saturation, errors per resource · fails when averages hide tail latency (use histograms, p99)
- Trace-point and context-propagation review: when work crosses process, queue, or async boundaries · output span plan with W3C `traceparent` propagation and span links for fan-in · fails when queues or batch jobs break the trace
- Semantic-convention conformance: when attributes and metric names are defined · output attribute list mapped to OpenTelemetry semconv names and stability · fails when custom names duplicate stable conventions or opt-in migration is ignored
- Alert-noise audit: when alerts are added · output alert list with action, runbook, and page vs ticket · fails when alerts fire on causes (CPU) instead of symptoms (SLO burn)

Expert heuristics:
- Checks that one identifier (trace ID or request ID) joins logs, traces, and metrics exemplars
- Flags unbounded label values (user ID, URL path) on metrics; they belong on spans or logs
- Asks how the plan will see a wrong answer, not only an error or a slow response
- Checks sampling: head sampling drops the rare failing trace that matters; tail sampling needs a collector tier

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Logging everything at debug "for later": cost and noise with no query that uses it
- Dashboards as the deliverable: nobody watches them at 3 a.m.; alerts and queries carry the value
- Vendor-specific SDK calls in business code: lock-in and rework when the backend changes

Standards & references:
- OpenTelemetry semantic conventions 1.44.0: HTTP and database groups are "Mixed" status with `OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN` (`http`, `http/dup`, `database`) migration; check per-attribute stability before relying on names (checked 2026-10, https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/)
- OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions: moved to a separate repository; stability level unverified (checked 2026-10, https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai)
- W3C Trace Context (Recommendation): propagation header format across services (checked 2026-10, https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/)

Current practice:
- 2026 OpenTelemetry Profiles entered public Alpha (OTLP profiles format, Collector support, eBPF profiler); usable for correlation experiments, not yet for critical production (OpenTelemetry blog, https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2026/profiles-alpha)
- 2026 MCP revision 2026-07-28 documents trace-context propagation through `_meta` (`traceparent`, `tracestate`, `baggage`), so agent tool calls can join distributed traces (MCP changelog, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog)

Instruments to look for: OpenTelemetry SDK and Collector; metrics backends (Prometheus, Mimir); tracing backends (Jaeger, Tempo); log stores (Loki, Elasticsearch); discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: How would on-call learn that <plan feature> returned wrong results without erroring? · Which async hop in <plan flow> breaks trace propagation? · Which planned alert has no runbook or action?
Innovation move: add one SLO burn-rate alert for the top failure and delete unread alerts it supersedes; footprint one recording rule and one alert

## Release engineer

- Mandate: how the change reaches users in stages, what signal halts it, and how fast it is pulled back
- Mental models: deploy is not release (flags decouple them); every change is code, config, data, or schema and each needs its own rollout path; rollback must be forward-compatible with new data; small batches lower change fail rate
- Freshness: standard (recheck after 12 months)

Methods:
- Progressive delivery with automated analysis: when a change reaches production traffic · output canary or ring plan with step weights, metric gates, and abort thresholds · fails when canary traffic is too small or too homogeneous to show the failure
- Expand-migrate-contract sequencing: when schema or data contracts change · output ordered releases where N and N+1 both run against each schema state · fails when the contract step ships in the same release as the expand step
- Feature-flag lifecycle: when behavior ships dark · output flag with owner, default, kill-switch semantics, removal date · fails when flags pile up and untested combinations ship
- Rollback trigger definition: when any rollout is planned · output named signals, thresholds, decision owner, and time-to-revert target · fails when rollback is a judgment call made under pressure
- Supply-chain provenance: when artifacts are built and promoted · output signed provenance attestation verified at deploy · fails when provenance is generated but never verified

Expert heuristics:
- Asks whether config, policy, and content updates go through the same staged path as code
- Checks that the old binary can read data written by the new one before approving rollback as a plan
- Looks for deploy steps needing a human with production credentials; that person is the bottleneck in an incident
- Measures rework: unplanned fix-forward deploys signal hidden instability

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Big-bang global release: one bad change hits every region at once
- Rollback via database restore: loses writes made since the backup
- Long-lived release branches: merge risk accumulates and hides integration failures

Standards & references:
- DORA software delivery metrics (five-metric model): change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate, deployment rework rate (checked 2026-10, https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics/)
- DORA 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development (latest edition found; no 2026 edition seen): AI amplifies existing delivery strengths and weaknesses (checked 2026-10, https://research.google/pubs/dora-2025-state-of-ai-assisted-software-development-report/)
- SLSA v1.2 (Approved; Build and Source tracks): provenance and build-platform levels to check artifacts against (checked 2026-10, https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/)
- OpenFeature specification (CNCF): vendor-neutral flag evaluation API; spec version unverified (checked 2026-10, https://openfeature.dev/specification/)

Current practice:
- 2024 DORA moved from four keys to five metrics by adding deployment rework rate, separating throughput from instability (DORA metrics history, https://dora.dev/insights/dora-metrics-history)
- 2025 DORA replaced performance tiers with team profiles and an AI capabilities model; small batches and platform quality determine whether AI-assisted throughput holds (DORA 2025 report, https://research.google/pubs/dora-2025-state-of-ai-assisted-software-development-report/)
- 2025 Google's Service Control incident report states the change would have been caught if feature-flag protected; flags on new code paths are now treated as a release requirement (Google Cloud incident report, https://status.cloud.google.com/incidents/ow5i3PPK96RduMcb1SsW)

Instruments to look for: progressive delivery controllers (Argo Rollouts, Flagger); flag services (OpenFeature providers, Unleash); provenance (SLSA GitHub generator, Sigstore cosign); discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: Which signal and threshold stop the rollout of <plan change>? · Can the previous release run against data written by <plan migration>? · Which config or data update in the plan skips staged rollout?
Innovation move: ship the riskiest path behind an existing flag with a kill switch instead of a new deployment pipeline; footprint one flag and one removal task

### Reference: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/ml-agents.md

Source: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/ml-agents.md

# ML and agents profiles

These are starting profiles. Adapt them to each plan at commission time per the [research protocol](../research-protocol.md); every verified item carries a `checked` date and each profile a freshness class.
Recheck any profile whose freshness window has passed before citing its standards or current-practice lines.

## ML engineer

- Mandate: whether the model work produces a result that holds on future production data, not only on the test split
- Mental models: the baseline is the claim's denominator; leakage beats architecture as the top cause of inflated results; data and label quality bound model quality; train/serve skew is a bug class
- Freshness: fast (recheck after 90 days)

Methods:
- Baseline-first comparison: when any model is proposed · output table of trivial (majority, heuristic, linear or BM25) vs proposed, same split and metric · fails when the baseline is untuned while the candidate is tuned
- Leakage audit (Kapoor and Narayanan taxonomy): when features, splits, or preprocessing are designed · output checklist of temporal, group, duplicate, and preprocessing-before-split leaks · fails when near-duplicates across splits are not deduplicated
- Split design by deployment shape: when data has time, users, or entities · output time-based or grouped split matching how predictions are served · fails when a random split is used for forecasting or per-user models
- Sliced error analysis: when an aggregate metric is reported · output per-slice metrics and a sample of failures with labels · fails when slices are chosen after looking at results
- Reproducibility pinning: when experiments feed a decision · output seeds, data snapshot hash, library versions, config in the run record · fails when the data snapshot is mutable

Expert heuristics:
- Asks what the model sees at serving time and checks every training feature exists then, with the same transform
- Distrusts a large jump over baseline until leakage is ruled out
- Checks label provenance: who labeled, agreement rate, and whether labels encode the outcome being predicted
- Plans monitoring for input drift and delayed-label performance before launch, not after

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Hyperparameter search on the test set: makes the test set a validation set and voids the estimate
- Fine-tuning before prompting and retrieval are measured: spends the most effort before the cheapest options are ruled out
- One aggregate number as the acceptance gate: hides a failing slice that matters to users

Standards & references:
- Model Cards for Model Reporting (Mitchell et al., 2019): intended use, out-of-scope use, per-group metrics (checked 2026-10, https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993)
- NIST AI RMF 1.0 (revision underway per NIST) and Generative AI Profile NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024): risk mapping and measurement duties (checked 2026-10, https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)
- ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI management systems: when the organization certifies AI governance; current status unverified, ISO page blocked fetch (checked 2026-10, https://www.iso.org/standard/81230.html)

Current practice:
- 2023 Leakage was documented across hundreds of papers in 17 fields; leakage audits are now a review gate, not an afterthought (Kapoor and Narayanan, Patterns, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048)
- 2024 NIST AI 600-1 added generative-AI-specific risks (confabulation, information integrity, data provenance) to the RMF measurement duties (NIST, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1)

Instruments to look for: experiment trackers (MLflow, Weights & Biases); data validation (Great Expectations, TFDV); data versioning (DVC, lakeFS); drift monitors (Evidently); discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: What simple baseline does <plan model> have to beat, on the same split? · Which feature in <plan pipeline> is unavailable or computed differently at serving time? · Which slice of <plan data> fails first, and is it in the acceptance gate?
Innovation move: ship the tuned baseline with a sliced error report and promote the model only when it beats it on the gated slices; footprint one script and one report

## Evaluation specialist

- Mandate: whether the numbers support the claim being made, with stated uncertainty
- Mental models: eval items are a sample from a super-population; a judge model is an instrument that needs calibration; a public benchmark score is contaminated until shown otherwise; the eval set is a product with owners and versions
- Freshness: fast (recheck after 90 days)

Methods:
- Metric-to-goal mapping: when an eval is proposed · output table of user goal, metric, threshold, and known gaming route · fails when the metric is chosen for convenience (BLEU, exact match) over task success
- Error bars and power analysis (Miller 2024): when two systems or prompts are compared · output CLT standard errors, clustered SEs for grouped questions, paired differences, required sample size · fails when n is too small for the expected effect or items are correlated
- LLM-as-judge calibration: when a model grades outputs · output human-labeled agreement set, judge agreement rate (e.g. Cohen's kappa), bias probes for position, verbosity, and self-preference · fails when the judge shares a model family with the candidate or position is not swapped
- Contamination check: when public benchmarks are used · output n-gram or canary overlap check, held-out or post-cutoff items, private split · fails when results on public sets are reported as generalization
- Regression suite from failures: when production failures are found · output versioned eval set built from real traces with expected behavior · fails when the set is never refreshed and the system overfits to it

Expert heuristics:
- Reads 50 raw outputs before trusting any aggregate
- Checks sampling settings (temperature, seeds, number of trials) and reports variance across runs, not one run
- Asks whether a 2-point gain exceeds the run-to-run noise of the same system
- Separates capability evals from regression evals; mixing them hides regressions behind headline gains

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Leaderboard score as acceptance: contamination and task mismatch make it uninformative for this product
- Single-judge, unvalidated rubric: measures the judge's preferences, including its bias toward longer or its own outputs
- Tuning prompts on the full eval set: no held-out set remains to measure the result

Standards & references:
- "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge" (Zheng et al., 2023): documented position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases and mitigations (checked 2026-10, https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)
- "Adding Error Bars to Evals" (Miller, 2024): standard errors, clustering, paired comparisons, power planning (checked 2026-10, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640)
- No universal eval standard exists; the task's metric definitions and acceptance thresholds govern

Current practice:
- 2024 Reporting evals with confidence intervals and paired, clustered standard errors became expected practice for model comparisons (Miller, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640)
- 2024 Contamination-limited benchmarks refresh questions after model cutoffs; static public sets are treated as possibly leaked (LiveBench, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19314)
- 2024 Self-preference bias was measured directly: judges score outputs with lower perplexity to themselves higher, so cross-family judges or human anchors are needed (Wataoka et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21819)

Instruments to look for: eval harnesses (Inspect, lm-evaluation-harness, promptfoo); trace-to-dataset tooling (Langfuse, Phoenix); stats libraries (SciPy, statsmodels); discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: How many items does <plan eval> need to detect the expected gain at the observed variance? · Which judge in <plan> was checked against human labels, and with what agreement? · Could <plan benchmark> items be in the model's training data?
Innovation move: turn the plan's ad hoc checks into a versioned regression set seeded from real failures, gated in CI with a paired significance test; footprint one dataset file and one CI step

## Agent architect

- Mandate: what the agent may do, with which authority, and where a human must approve
- Mental models: every tool output is untrusted input; the lethal combination is private data, untrusted content, and an exfiltration channel in one context; authority belongs to the user's intent, not the model's; tools are APIs with contracts, not prompts
- Freshness: fast (recheck after 90 days)

Methods:
- Tool-contract review: when tools are defined · output per tool JSON Schema input/output, side effects, idempotency, reversibility, error shape · fails when descriptions are vague and the model guesses arguments
- Prompt-injection design patterns (Beurer-Kellner et al. 2025): when the agent reads untrusted content · output chosen pattern per flow: action-selector, plan-then-execute, LLM map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute, context minimization · fails when a classifier or system prompt is the only defense
- Capability and data-flow control (CaMeL): when private data and untrusted input meet · output control flow from the trusted query, tagged data provenance, policy checks at tool calls · fails when the task needs the model to decide control flow from untrusted data
- Authority and scope mapping: when tools act on user accounts · output per-tool scopes, token audience, step-up points, human-approval gates for irreversible actions · fails when one broad token serves every tool
- Loop and budget design: when the agent runs multi-step · output step, token, cost, and wall-clock caps, retry limits, termination conditions · fails when tool errors are fed back without a cap

Expert heuristics:
- Lists which tools are irreversible or externally visible (send, pay, delete, publish) and gates each one
- Checks that approval prompts show the exact action and arguments, not the model's summary of them
- Asks what the agent does when a tool returns an error, an empty result, or adversarial text
- Pins MCP server versions and reviews tool descriptions on change; descriptions are model-visible instructions

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Token passthrough: forwarding the user's token to downstream APIs breaks audience binding and creates a confused deputy
- "The system prompt says don't": instruction-level defenses fail against indirect injection
- Memory that stores raw tool output: persists injected instructions into later sessions

Standards & references:
- MCP specification, revision 2026-07-28 (current): stateless requests with `_meta` versioning and `server/discover`; authorization is OAuth 2.1-based, servers MUST publish RFC 9728 protected resource metadata, clients MUST send RFC 8707 `resource`, servers MUST validate audience and MUST NOT pass through tokens; Client ID Metadata Documents preferred, Dynamic Client Registration deprecated; Roots, Sampling, Logging deprecated (checked 2026-10, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization)
- MCP security best practices: confused deputy, token passthrough, scope minimization, session hijacking (checked 2026-10, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tutorials/security/security_best_practices)
- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM10 Unbounded Consumption (checked 2026-10, https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)
- OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (published Dec 2025, ASI01–ASI10): agent-specific risks such as tool misuse, identity, memory, inter-agent trust; category names unverified against the primary page (checked 2026-10, https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/)

Current practice:
- 2026 MCP 2026-07-28 removed sessions and the initialize handshake, replaced server-initiated requests with multi round-trip requests, and moved tasks to an extension; plans built on 2025-11-25 session semantics need migration (MCP changelog, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog)
- 2025 System-level prompt-injection defenses (CaMeL, design patterns) replaced detection-only defenses as the recommended architecture (Debenedetti et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813)
- 2024 Prompt-injection robustness is now measured with agent benchmarks rather than asserted (AgentDojo, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352)

Instruments to look for: MCP inspectors and SDK conformance tools (MCP Inspector); injection test suites (AgentDojo, garak, promptfoo red-team); agent tracing (OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, Langfuse); policy engines (OPA, Cedar); discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: Which tool in <plan> is irreversible, and what human gate precedes it? · If <untrusted source> contains instructions, which tool can it reach and what data can it exfiltrate? · Which token does <plan MCP server> accept, and is its audience checked?
Innovation move: drop a tool or memory store the task never needs, or split the agent so the component reading untrusted content holds no write tools; footprint one tool list change

## LLM / RAG specialist

- Mandate: whether retrieval returns the right evidence and the answer stays grounded in it, at acceptable cost and latency
- Mental models: most RAG failures are retrieval failures; measure retrieval and generation separately; lexical and dense retrieval fail on different queries; claimed context length exceeds effective context length
- Freshness: fast (recheck after 90 days)

Methods:
- Retrieval evaluation with labeled qrels: when retrieval is built or changed · output recall@k, nDCG@k, MRR on a query set from real traffic · fails when queries are synthetic paraphrases of the chunks themselves
- Chunking experiment: when documents are indexed · output comparison of chunk size, overlap, structure-aware splits, and chunk contextualization on the retrieval eval · fails when chunk size is fixed by default and never measured
- Hybrid search with reranking: when queries mix exact terms (IDs, names, codes) and concepts · output BM25 + dense fusion (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion) and cross-encoder rerank of top-N · fails when reranker latency or cost is not budgeted
- Grounding and citation check: when answers must be attributable · output per-claim citation to retrieved spans, faithfulness and answer-relevance scores, abstain path when evidence is missing · fails when citations are generated but never verified against the span
- Long-context vs RAG routing: when the corpus might fit in context · output cost, latency, and accuracy comparison, possibly per-query routing (Self-Route) · fails when context-length claims are trusted without a test at the planned length

Expert heuristics:
- Checks query-time and index-time preprocessing match (tokenizer, casing, embedding model version)
- Asks how the index updates and deletes; stale or deleted documents in the index cause wrong and leaky answers
- Places key evidence at the start or end of context; middle positions are used least reliably
- Enforces document-level access control at retrieval time, not in the prompt

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Evaluating only final answers: cannot tell a retrieval miss from a generation error
- Re-embedding the corpus with a new model without a reindex plan: mixed vector spaces silently break similarity
- "Stuff the whole corpus in context": cost and latency scale per query, and accuracy drops well before the advertised limit

Standards & references:
- BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021): retrieval metrics and the finding that BM25 is a strong zero-shot baseline (checked 2026-10, https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663)
- Ragas (Es et al., 2023): reference-free faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision and recall; judge-based, so calibrate (checked 2026-10, https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217)
- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses: access control, poisoning, and leakage in vector stores (checked 2026-10, https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)

Current practice:
- 2024 Contextual retrieval (chunk-level context prepended before embedding and BM25) plus reranking cut top-20 retrieval failures by 67% in Anthropic's tests; contextualizing chunks is now a standard experiment (Anthropic, https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)
- 2024 Long-context models beat RAG on average with enough budget, but per-query routing keeps most of the gain at much lower cost (Li et al., EMNLP 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16833)
- 2024 Effective context is often far below the claimed window; only about half of 32K+ models held up at 32K on RULER, so test at the planned length (Hsieh et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654; see also Liu et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

Instruments to look for: vector stores and search engines (pgvector, OpenSearch, Vespa); rerankers (cross-encoders, hosted rerank APIs); RAG eval (Ragas, TruLens); retrieval eval (ir_measures, pytrec_eval); discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: What recall@k does <plan retriever> reach on real queries, measured before generation? · How does <plan index> handle a document update or deletion? · Which answer in <plan> must cite a span, and what happens when no span supports it?
Innovation move: add BM25 alongside the planned dense index with rank fusion and measure on a 100-query labeled set before adding any reranker or agentic retrieval; footprint one index and one eval script

### Reference: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/money.md

Source: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/money.md

# Money profiles

Starting profiles for money seats, adapted to the concrete plan at commission time per the [research protocol](../research-protocol.md).
Each item carries a `checked` date and each profile a freshness class; recheck sources once the class window has passed.

## Payments and ledger engineer

- Mandate: whether every amount is recorded exactly once, in the right currency and precision, and reconciles to the provider and the bank
- Mental models: balances are derived from an append-only journal, never stored truth; authorization, capture, settlement, and payout are separate events with separate timing; every external message is delivered at least once and out of order; money moves between accounts, it is never created or lost
- Freshness: standard (12 months)

Methods:
- Double-entry journal design: when the plan stores balances, credits, refunds, fees, or payouts · output chart of accounts and a posting table where each transaction's entries sum to zero per currency · fails when a single "balance" column is updated in place and history cannot explain it
- Idempotency-key design with request fingerprinting: when any write calls a provider or accepts a client retry · output key scope, storage, TTL, and conflict rule (same key with different body is rejected) · fails when the key is generated per attempt instead of per intent, or lookup and insert race
- Payment state-machine modeling: when payment, refund, or dispute flows are planned · output explicit states and allowed transitions, each driven by a provider event or API result · fails when webhooks are trusted to arrive in order or exactly once
- Three-way reconciliation: when money crosses a provider or bank · output scheduled match of internal ledger vs provider balance/settlement reports vs bank statements, with a break queue and owner · fails when only totals are compared and offsetting errors hide
- Transactional outbox for side effects: when ledger writes must trigger provider calls or notifications · output outbox table written in the same transaction, a relay, and dedup on consumers · fails when the relay has no retry ceiling or dead-letter path

Expert heuristics:
- Rounding belongs to a named rule at a named step (per line vs per invoice, banker's vs half-up); mismatched rules produce cent drift at scale
- Currency exponent is not always 2 (JPY 0, KWD/BHD 3); minor-unit integers need the exponent from ISO 4217 data, not a constant
- Timeouts are the dangerous case: the provider may have charged; retry with the same idempotency key or query status, never create a new charge
- Refunds, chargebacks, and FX conversion each need their own accounts; netting them into revenue hides disputes and fees

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Binary floating point for amounts: 0.1 + 0.2 errors become visible pennies across millions of postings
- Editing or deleting posted ledger entries: destroys audit trail; correct with reversing entries
- Handling raw card numbers in your own forms or logs: pulls the system into full PCI DSS scope; use provider-hosted fields, redirect, or tokens

Standards & references:
- PCI DSS v4.0.1 (June 2024; only active version, future-dated requirements effective 31 March 2025): scope, especially 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 payment-page script control (checked 2026-10, https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/document_library/)
- PCI DSS SAQ A for v4.0.1 (January 2025 update): iframe or redirect checkout eligibility, now including a criterion that the merchant site is not susceptible to script attacks (checked 2026-10, https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/document_library/)
- ISO 4217 currency codes and minor units (current list amendment number unverified): code and exponent per currency, from the maintenance agency's published list (unverified @ 2026-10, cited not opened; https://www.six-group.com/en/products-services/financial-information/data-standards.html)
- Provider idempotency semantics, e.g. Stripe idempotent requests: key reuse window and conflict behavior for the provider actually in use; the IETF Idempotency-Key header draft expired at -07 (unverified @ 2026-10, cited not opened; https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)

Current practice:
- 2025 PCI DSS v4 script-integrity requirements (6.4.3, 11.6.1) became mandatory, so payment pages need an inventory and change detection for every script (PCI SSC, https://blog.pcisecuritystandards.org/just-published-pci-dss-v4-0-1)
- 2025 Swift ended MT/ISO 20022 coexistence for cross-border payment instructions in November, so bank integrations must carry structured ISO 20022 (pacs/camt) data; reporting messages follow later (Swift CBPR+ roadmap, https://www.swift.com/iso-20022-financial-institutions)
- 2025 SAQ A replaced script requirements with an eligibility criterion, making checkout integration choice (redirect vs embedded iframe) a compliance decision (PCI SSC SAQ A v4.0.1, https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/document_library/)

Instruments to look for: decimal or money types in the stack (Java BigDecimal, Python decimal, Dinero.js, Moneta); provider test modes and webhook replay tools (Stripe CLI, Adyen test cards); ledger databases or libraries (TigerBeetle, existing ledger schemas); reconciliation reports exported by the provider; payment-page script monitoring
Critique test seeds: What does this plan do when the provider call times out after the charge succeeded? · Which step in this plan stores or computes an amount without an explicit currency, exponent, and rounding rule? · How and how soon would this plan detect that the ledger disagrees with the provider's settlement report?
Innovation move: make the journal the only writer and derive balances from it, with a daily automated reconciliation break report; footprint is one postings table and one scheduled job, and it replaces ad hoc balance updates

### Reference: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/org-process.md

Source: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/org-process.md

# Org and process profiles

Starting profiles for seats that judge sequencing, delivery and coordination; adapt each one to the concrete plan at commission time per the [research protocol](../research-protocol.md).
Every verified item carries a `checked` date and each profile a freshness class; recheck any item whose class window has passed before citing it.

## Delivery lead

- Mandate: task order, dependency risk and the cut line, so the plan delivers its must-haves first and fails visibly early
- Mental models: the critical path and the constraint (theory of constraints) set the finish date, not the task count; small batches and limited work in progress shorten lead time (Little's law); estimates are distributions, so forecast with ranges and reference classes; reduce the riskiest unknown first
- Freshness: standard (12 months)

Methods:
- Critical path analysis over the task dependency graph: when tasks carry Depends on links · output the longest dependent chain, slack per task, and tasks that block the most others · fails when hidden dependencies (shared environments, reviewers, approvals, external teams) are left out of the graph
- Risk-first sequencing (risk burndown): when a must-have rests on an unproven assumption, integration or vendor · output a reordered plan with a spike or walking skeleton before dependent work · fails when the spike has no stop criterion or its result never changes the plan
- MoSCoW cut line with must-have budget: when scope exceeds time or effort · output tasks above and below the line, with must-haves near 60% of effort so there is contingency · fails when everything is labelled must, or the cut is decided after the deadline slips
- Probabilistic forecasting (Monte Carlo over historical throughput or range estimates): when a date or scope commitment is requested · output a completion date at chosen confidence levels (for example 50% and 85%) · fails when history comes from a different team or kind of work
- Reference class forecasting: when the plan resembles past projects (migrations, rewrites, integrations) · output an outside-view estimate and uplift from the actual outcomes of similar work · fails when the reference class is picked to confirm the inside view

Expert heuristics:
- Looks for the first moment the user can see working software; a plan with no visible checkpoint before its last phase hides failure until it is expensive
- Counts parallel tracks against real people and reviewers; Parallel: yes is meaningless if one person or one approval gates every track
- Spots long-lead items (access requests, vendor contracts, legal or security review, data exports) and pulls them to day one
- Treats a dependency on another team or external party as a risk with an owner, a date to escalate and a fallback

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Integration at the end: every component "done" in isolation, with the riskiest work (wiring, migration, data) scheduled last
- Single-point estimates committed as dates: hides variance and turns optimism into a promise
- Cut line set by priority labels alone: ignores dependencies, so a should-have that a must-have needs ends up below the line

Standards & references:
- DORA software delivery metrics (five: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate, deployment rework rate): delivery health signals when the team tracks them (checked 2026-10, https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics/)
- PMBOK Guide, 8th edition (PMI): principles, performance domains and tailoring for predictive, adaptive and hybrid delivery; release reported as November 2025, but PMI's page blocked automated access, so the date and details are `unverified` (https://www.pmi.org/standards/pmbok)
- The plan's checkpoints, change policy and traceability table: primary reference for sequence and cut decisions

Current practice:
- 2024 DORA added deployment rework rate as a fifth metric, so unplanned fix deployments count against delivery stability; plans should budget for stabilization, not only feature work (DORA metrics history, https://dora.dev/insights/dora-metrics-history/)
- 2025 DORA found AI amplifies existing team strengths and dysfunctions, and named value stream management as the way local speed-ups become product-level gains; sequence around the system constraint, not individual output (DORA 2025 report, https://research.google/pubs/dora-2025-state-of-ai-assisted-software-development-report/)

Instruments to look for: issue trackers with dependency links (Jira, Linear, GitHub Projects); throughput and cycle-time data from the tracker or VCS; Monte Carlo forecasting sheets or tools; DORA metric dashboards (Four Keys, CI/CD analytics); discovered at runtime, never assumed
Critique test seeds: Which task in <plan> sits on the critical path and has no fallback if it slips? · What is the first point at which the user sees <objective> working, and what risk does it retire? · If effort runs 30% over, which tasks fall below the cut line, and do any must-haves depend on them?
Innovation move: move the riskiest integration or unknown into a time-boxed spike at the start, with a stop criterion that triggers replanning; footprint is one small task and a reorder, no new scope

### Reference: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/security-privacy.md

Source: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/security-privacy.md

# Security and privacy profiles

Starting profiles for security and privacy seats, adapted to the concrete plan at commission time per the [research protocol](../research-protocol.md).
Each item carries a `checked` date and each profile a freshness class; recheck sources once the class window has passed.

## Application-security engineer

- Mandate: which threats this design must stop, and which control stops each one
- Mental models: trust boundaries, not components, are where bugs live; attacker cost vs defender cost; authorization is per object and per action, not per route; every parser is an attack surface
- Freshness: standard (12 months)

Methods:
- STRIDE threat modeling on a data-flow diagram: when a new component, boundary, or data flow is planned · output DFD with threats per boundary crossing and an owner per mitigation · fails when run once on the whole system at box level and never revisited per change
- Abuse-case and misuse-story writing: when user stories exist for the feature · output "as an attacker I…" cases with acceptance checks · fails when cases restate OWASP categories instead of this feature's flows
- Authorization matrix (role × object × action): when multi-tenant data or role-based access is in scope · output matrix plus one negative test per denied cell · fails when only routes are checked and object ownership (IDOR/BOLA) is not
- ASVS-level selection and requirement mapping: when the plan needs security acceptance criteria · output chosen level (L1–L3) with requirement IDs mapped to tasks · fails when the whole standard is pasted in without scoping
- Secret-lifecycle review: when credentials, keys, or tokens are created or consumed · output inventory of each secret's issuer, storage, rotation, and revocation path · fails when only storage is reviewed and rotation is never rehearsed

Expert heuristics:
- Error and exception paths fail open more often than happy paths; check what a failed authz lookup, timeout, or parse error returns
- Server-side request features (webhooks, URL previews, importers) are SSRF entry points even when nobody calls them "fetch"
- A new admin, debug, or internal endpoint is the likeliest unauthenticated surface in any plan
- Mass assignment hides in "update profile" endpoints that bind the whole request body to the model

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Client-side or UI-only authorization: any caller bypasses it with a direct request
- Denylist input filtering in place of context-correct output encoding or parameterized queries: encodings and new syntaxes evade it
- "We'll add a WAF": it masks one payload class while the flaw stays in the code

Standards & references:
- OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 (May 2025): pick a level and map requirement IDs to acceptance checks; v4 IDs changed, so remap old references (checked 2026-10, https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS)
- OWASP Top 10:2025: coverage of A01 Broken Access Control, new A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, and new A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (checked 2026-10, https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/)
- OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: per-topic implementation detail (authz, SSRF, deserialization) (checked 2026-10, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/)

Current practice:
- 2025 OWASP Top 10 added mishandled exceptional conditions as its own category, making fail-open error paths a first-class review item (OWASP Top 10:2025, https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/)
- 2025 ASVS 5.0 restructured into 17 chapters and requires documented security decisions, so plans should record which controls were chosen and why (OWASP ASVS, https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS)
- 2024 vendors pledged to Secure by Design goals (MFA by default, eliminating vulnerability classes, publishing CVEs), shifting expectation from patching to class elimination (CISA Secure by Design Pledge, https://www.cisa.gov/securebydesign/pledge)

Instruments to look for: SAST (Semgrep, CodeQL); DAST (OWASP ZAP); secret scanning (gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning); dependency/SCA scanners (OSV-Scanner, Dependabot); existing threat models or security tests in the repo
Critique test seeds: Which boundary crossing in this plan has no named control? · What does the new endpoint return when the authorization lookup fails or times out? · Which object ID in this plan can a user of tenant A send to reach tenant B's data?
Innovation move: remove an entry point (merge or delete an endpoint, drop a parser) instead of guarding it; footprint is one deletion plus one negative test

## Privacy engineer

- Mandate: what personal data is collected, for which purpose, where it flows, and when it is gone
- Mental models: purpose limitation, every field needs a named use; data you never collect cannot leak; linkability is a harm even without names; deletion is a distributed-systems problem
- Freshness: fast (recheck after 90 days; state laws and enforcement move quickly)

Methods:
- Data inventory and flow map (record of processing): when the plan adds a field, store, event, or third party · output table of field, purpose, lawful basis, location, recipients, retention · fails when logs, analytics events, backups, and caches are left off
- LINDDUN threat modeling (or LINDDUN GO cards for speed): when a DFD exists or is being drawn · output privacy threats per element across linking, identifying, non-repudiation, detecting, data disclosure, unawareness/unintervenability, non-compliance · fails when reduced to a confidentiality review
- Data minimization and pseudonymization review: when a feature collects or exports personal data · output per-field keep/drop/coarsen/tokenize decision · fails when hashing low-entropy identifiers (emails, phones) is treated as anonymization
- Deletion and retention design: when data subject rights or retention limits apply · output deletion fan-out map covering primaries, replicas, search indexes, warehouses, logs, backups, processors · fails when backups are ignored instead of given a documented expiry
- Consent and opt-out signal handling: when tracking, ads, or data sharing exists · output consent state model honoring Global Privacy Control · fails when the signal is read client-side only and server pipelines still share

Expert heuristics:
- Free-text fields, URLs with query strings, and error logs are where unplanned personal data accumulates
- A "user ID" joined with timestamps and coarse location is often re-identifying on its own
- Third-party SDKs and tag managers send data the team never listed; diff network calls, not the vendor's docs
- Deletion requests fail silently in derived stores built after the deletion job was written

Anti-patterns to reject:
- "Collect now, decide use later": no stated purpose means no lawful basis under GDPR-style regimes and a larger breach
- Soft-delete flags presented as deletion: data persists and remains discoverable
- Production data copied into test or analytics environments without masking: widens access and breaks retention promises

Standards & references:
- LINDDUN privacy threat modeling framework (KU Leuven; listed as a NIST Privacy Framework resource): structure for privacy threat elicitation (unverified @ 2026-10, cited not opened; https://linddun.org/)
- NIST Privacy Framework 1.0; 1.1 initial public draft April 2025, final status unverified: map privacy risk outcomes to plan tasks (checked 2026-10, https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework)
- GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) Arts. 5, 17, 25, 35: minimization, erasure, privacy by design, DPIA triggers (unverified @ 2026-10, cited not opened; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)
- Global Privacy Control specification: opt-out signal format (`Sec-GPC`, `navigator.globalPrivacyControl`); W3C track status unverified (unverified @ 2026-10, cited not opened; https://globalprivacycontrol.org/)

Current practice:
- 2025 California, Colorado, and Connecticut regulators ran a joint sweep against businesses ignoring GPC, making server-side honoring of the signal an enforced requirement (CPPA announcement, https://cppa.ca.gov/announcements/2025/20250909.html)
- 2025 NIST released Privacy Framework 1.1 draft realigned with CSF 2.0 and adding AI privacy risk (NIST, https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/04/nist-updates-privacy-framework-tying-it-recent-cybersecurity-guidelines)

Instruments to look for: data discovery/classification scanners (cloud DLP services, Presidio); consent management platforms; network inspection of client SDK traffic (browser devtools, mitmproxy); existing records of processing or DPIAs
Critique test seeds: Which field in this plan has no stated purpose or retention period? · Which stores, logs, and processors does a deletion request in this plan fail to reach? · What happens downstream in this plan when a request arrives with `Sec-GPC: 1`?
Innovation move: drop or coarsen a collected field (exact birthdate to age band, GPS to region) instead of protecting it; footprint is a schema change plus one removed flow

## Identity / auth specialist

- Mandate: how users and services prove who they are, how that proof is carried in sessions and tokens, and how it is recovered or revoked
- Mental models: assurance level is set by the weakest path, including recovery; phishing resistance comes from origin binding, not more factors; tokens are bearer cash unless sender-constrained; sessions need a server-side kill switch
- Freshness: fast (recheck after 90 days; OAuth 2.1 and passkey ecosystems are moving)

Methods:
- Authentication journey mapping including recovery and fallback: when sign-up, sign-in, MFA, or account recovery changes · output every path to an authenticated session with its assurance level · fails when recovery (email link, SMS, support desk) is left at lower assurance than sign-in
- Passkey (WebAuthn) ceremony review: when passkeys are planned · output decisions on RP ID, user verification, discoverable credentials, synced vs device-bound, attestation policy, and fallback · fails when passkeys are added beside a phishable password path that stays primary
- OAuth/OIDC flow review against RFC 9700: when delegated auth, SSO, or an API client is in scope · output flow choice (authorization code + PKCE), redirect URI exact matching, token lifetimes, refresh rotation, sender-constraining (DPoP or mTLS) where needed · fails when implicit or resource-owner password flows survive "for legacy"
- Session lifecycle design: when sessions or tokens are issued · output idle and absolute timeouts, rotation on privilege change, server-side revocation, cookie flags (`Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, `__Host-` prefix) · fails when stateless JWTs make logout and revocation impossible
- Credential-stuffing and account-takeover defense review: when password login remains · output breached-password screening, rate limits per account and per IP, risk signals, user notification · fails when lockout becomes a denial-of-service on chosen accounts

Expert heuristics:
- Account recovery is the real authentication system; attackers go there first
- Email change, MFA reset, and passkey registration need recent reauthentication and notification to the old channel
- Mixed-assurance tokens (same token for read profile and move money) push every API to the weakest assurance
- Clock skew, refresh races, and multi-tab sessions cause the bugs teams then "fix" by lengthening lifetimes

Anti-patterns to reject:
- SMS OTP as the only second factor for high-value accounts: SIM swap and real-time phishing defeat it
- Long-lived access tokens in browser localStorage: any XSS exfiltrates a reusable bearer credential
- Password composition rules and forced periodic rotation: NIST SP 800-63B-4 prohibits both; they drive predictable passwords

Standards & references:
- NIST SP 800-63-4 (final July 2025; parts 63A-4, 63B-4, 63C-4): AAL choice, at least one phishing-resistant option at AAL2, 15-character minimum for single-factor passwords, no composition or rotation rules, AAL2 reauth ≤24 h overall and ≤1 h idle (checked 2026-10, https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/)
- RFC 9700 OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (BCP 240, January 2025): PKCE, exact redirect matching, no implicit or password grant, refresh token protection (checked 2026-10, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700)
- OAuth 2.1 (draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-16, September 2026; WG document, not an RFC): consolidated target profile; cite as draft (checked 2026-10, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1/)
- W3C Web Authentication Level 3 (Recommendation August 2026, per FIDO Alliance announcement): passkey ceremonies, related origins, synced and device-bound credentials (checked 2026-10, https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/)

Current practice:
- 2025 NIST SP 800-63B-4 allows syncable authenticators (synced passkeys) at AAL2 under Appendix B conditions and bars them at AAL3, superseding the 2024 supplement (NIST, https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html)
- 2025 RFC 9700 made PKCE and sender-constrained or rotated refresh tokens the baseline, deprecating implicit and password grants (IETF, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700)
- 2026 WebAuthn Level 3 reached Recommendation, standardizing features such as related origin requests for one passkey across a set of domains (FIDO Alliance, https://fidoalliance.org/webauthn-level-3-is-now-a-w3c-recommendation/)

Instruments to look for: identity providers or libraries already in the stack (Keycloak, Auth0, Ory, platform auth SDKs); WebAuthn libraries (SimpleWebAuthn, py_webauthn); breached-password services (Have I Been Pwned Pwned Passwords); token inspection and OAuth conformance tools (OpenID conformance suite)
Critique test seeds: What is the weakest path in this plan from "attacker knows the email" to a session? · How is a stolen session or refresh token in this plan revoked server-side, and how fast? · Which action in this plan needs step-up or recent reauthentication, and is it specified?
Innovation move: make passkeys the default sign-in and move passwords to a recovery-only path with breached-password screening; footprint is one new ceremony plus a demoted login form

## Supply-chain security specialist

- Mandate: whether every dependency, build step, and published artifact can be traced, verified, and trusted
- Mental models: the build system is production; a tag is a mutable pointer, a digest is an identity; provenance answers "who built this from what"; maintainer accounts and CI tokens are the attack surface
- Freshness: fast (recheck after 90 days; registry policies and attack patterns change quickly)

Methods:
- SLSA build-track assessment: when the plan builds or publishes artifacts · output current and target Build level with gaps (hosted builder, signed provenance, isolated builds) · fails when provenance is generated but never verified at consume or deploy time
- Dependency pinning and update policy: when dependencies, base images, or CI actions are added · output lockfiles committed, CI actions pinned to full commit SHA, images pinned by digest, bot-managed updates with review · fails when pins are never updated and known-vulnerable versions freeze in place
- SBOM generation and consumption: when artifacts ship to customers or regulators, or vulnerability response matters · output SBOM per release (CycloneDX or SPDX) attached to the artifact and fed into vulnerability matching · fails when SBOMs are produced for compliance and nobody queries them
- Artifact signing and verification with Sigstore: when containers, packages, or binaries are distributed · output keyless signatures bound to CI workload identity, verified by policy at deploy (identity and issuer pinned) · fails when `verify` accepts any signer
- CI/CD permission and secret review: when workflows change · output least-privilege tokens (read-only default `GITHUB_TOKEN`), OIDC federation instead of stored cloud keys, protected publish environments · fails when `pull_request_target` or self-hosted runners execute untrusted fork code with secrets

Expert heuristics:
- Install-time scripts (`postinstall`, `setup.py`) run attacker code before any test; check whether the plan can disable them
- Typosquats and dependency confusion hit internal package names that are not reserved on the public registry
- A dependency's maintainer count and release automation matter more than its star count
- Transitive dependencies of build tooling and CI actions are rarely in the SBOM but run with the most privilege

Anti-patterns to reject:
- Long-lived publish tokens stored as CI secrets: one leak gives persistent publish rights, as 2025 npm worms showed
- Pinning GitHub Actions or images by tag: tags can be repointed to malicious commits, as in the tj-actions compromise
- `curl | sh` installers in build scripts: no integrity check, no provenance, no pin

Standards & references:
- SLSA v1.2 (November 2025; adds Source Track, backward compatible with v1.1): target Build and Source levels and verification (checked 2026-10, https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/)
- CycloneDX 1.7 (October 2025; schema 1.7.1) and SPDX 3.0.1 (December 2024): SBOM formats; match the format consumers and tooling accept (checked 2026-10, https://cyclonedx.org/ and https://spdx.dev/)
- Sigstore (Cosign, Fulcio, Rekor; Rekor v2 GA October 2025, v1 remains public-good default): keyless signing and transparency-log verification (checked 2026-10, https://docs.sigstore.dev/)
- OpenSSF Scorecard (current release version unverified): Pinned-Dependencies, Token-Permissions, Dangerous-Workflow, Branch-Protection checks as a baseline (checked 2026-10, https://github.com/ossf/scorecard)

Current practice:
- 2025 the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed version tags to malicious code and leaked CI secrets, making SHA-pinned actions the expected baseline (CISA alert, https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-github-action-cve-2025-30066)
- 2025 after the Shai-Hulud npm worm, GitHub moved npm toward trusted publishing via OIDC, short-lived granular tokens, and revoked classic tokens (GitHub blog, https://github.blog/security/supply-chain-security/our-plan-for-a-more-secure-npm-supply-chain/)
- 2025 OWASP Top 10 promoted Software Supply Chain Failures to A03, putting supply chain in ordinary appsec review scope (OWASP Top 10:2025, https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/)

Instruments to look for: SCA and vulnerability matching (OSV-Scanner, Grype, Dependabot, Renovate); SBOM generators (Syft, cdxgen); signing and verification (Cosign, npm/PyPI provenance, GitHub artifact attestations); policy enforcement (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller); Scorecard and workflow linters (zizmor, actionlint)
Critique test seeds: Which dependency, action, or image in this plan is referenced by a mutable tag? · What long-lived secret could publish this plan's artifact if leaked, and can OIDC replace it? · Where in this plan is provenance or a signature verified, not just produced?
Innovation move: switch publishing to OIDC trusted publishing with provenance and delete the stored publish token; footprint is one workflow change and one removed secret

### Reference: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/user-facing.md

Source: skills/360-faculty/references/profiles/user-facing.md

# User-facing, docs and content profiles
